pr_title: [Https] Various improvements to the dev-certs tool
pr_body:
* Support exporting the certificate in PEM format without a key.
* Bump the certificate version number to `2` and ensure the certificate with the highest version is picked moving forward.
* Add support for the `--trust` option in the command-line on Linux and emit a message pointing to the documentation page with instructions on how to trust the certificate on different Linux distributions manually.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/21266 https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/23776
pr_comments:
Kestrel is now failing to find a dev cert. I tried regenerating the dev cert using `dotnet dev-certs https --trust` using the `5.0.100-rc.1.20379.10` SDK (the SDK currently used in `master` and `release/5.0`) only to see it incorrectly claim that "A valid HTTPS certificate is already present." I manually debugged through GetCertificateVersion in CertificateManager and saw that my dev cert was so old that our dev cert validation logic couldn't even find a version.

When I manually deleted the existing dev cert, the tool did create a new dev cert in a new location (under "Trusted Root CA" instead of "Personal" in certmgr), but it only created version 1 of the dev cert which Kestrel is still unhappy with. I turns out the SDK our repo is using is simply too old, but that was hard to figure out based on the following log:

```
Unable to locate an appropriate development https certificate.
Unhandled exception. System.InvalidOperationException: Unable to configure HTTPS endpoint. No server certificate was specified, and the default developer certificate could not be found or is out of date.
To generate a developer certificate run 'dotnet dev-certs https'. To trust the certificate (Windows and macOS only) run 'dotnet dev-certs https --trust'.
```

And then when I did run 'dotnet dev-certs https --trust':

```
> dotnet dev-certs https --trust
Trusting the HTTPS development certificate was requested. A confirmation prompt will be displayed if the certificate was not previously trusted. Click yes on the prompt to trust the certificate.
A valid HTTPS certificate is already present.
```

Can this experience be improved somehow to tell customers to update the SDK? I get that using newer runtimes than SDKs is unusual, but it isn't terribly difficult to update to a new runtime without updating the SDK. I worry that this will be hard for developers to track down. @MackinnonBuck ran into this on Friday. I was able to fix the issue on my end by installing the `5.0.100-rc.1.20424.6` SDK, but not before I wasted a bunch of time investigating. @javiercn @Tratcher @davidfowl
I also noticed this Friday in some unrelated samples but didn't have time to investigate. It's pretty awkward when Kestrel and VS disagree weather or not you have a current dev cert.
I'll look at this tomorrow, though I'm not sure what we could do about it. We want to pick the certificate with the highest version available. This might as well be a point in time issue.
Should we allow kestrel to load an old dev cert if a new one isn't available?

> Should we allow kestrel to load an old dev cert if a new one isn't available?

I don't think so, that can cause problems. For example, on Mac OS we have an issue with the certificate 3.1 installs on some machines, and we switched the approach in 5.0 and made this change to make sure we create a new certificate using the new way and that Kestrel picks that one instead of the "broken" one.

I don't see how that invalidates the option for scenarios we know would work. Sure, the old mac cert was broken and we could choose not to load it, but that doesn't have to affect what we do on Windows.

> I don't see how that invalidates the option for scenarios we know would work. Sure, the old mac cert was broken and we could choose not to load it, but that doesn't have to affect what we do on Windows.

But we want in general to load the newer cert so that we don't have to deal with patching old runtimes when things like these happen.

If we had to choose between optimizing for this scenario or optimizing for developing using a runtime that is newer than the SDK, I would say we would optimize for the first one. 

The second scenario is not a supported scenario (we don't support targeting newer runtimes with older SDKs) and hence it's not going to be common. The issues we are experiencing right now are an artifact of our build system.

issue_context.title: [Https] Certificate trust on linux
issue_context.body: Figure out the required steps to make this work (at least for Ubuntu) and remove any potential existing issues.
comments: Javier, I'm trying to figure out how to do this on Fedora. Can you detail the steps you took?

@aloh86 I don't have specific steps.

This issue is for tracking future work, but we haven't actually started on this.
The plan here is to allow the "--trust" flag on Linux but print a link to a docs page where we will add per-distro instructions on how to do this.

review_comments:
```suggestion
                    reporter.Warn("Trusting the HTTPS development certificate was requested. Trusting the certificate on Linux distributions automatically is not supported. " +
                        "For instructions on how to manually trust the certificate on your Linux distribution, go to https://aka.ms/dev-certs-trust");
```
